retrieved.body:
Account day. Today was about the account itself and the scary all-powerful login.

- A new AWS account starts with exactly one identity: the **root user**. That's the email and password I
  signed up with, and it has complete access to every service and resource in the account.
- The account itself is identified by a 12-digit **account ID**.
- Rule number one: don't use root for everyday work. Save it for the root-only tasks, like changing the
  account's email or the root password, closing the account, and some billing and tax settings. What to use
  *instead* for daily work, I don't know yet. I'm guessing the IAM days get into it somehow?
- **MFA on root is required now**, for every kind of account. You have to register it within 35 days of your
  first console sign-in attempt.
- Supported MFA types:
  - passkeys and security keys (FIDO), which AWS recommends
  - virtual authenticator apps (the 6-digit TOTP codes)
  - hardware TOTP tokens
- Lots of older tutorials still say MFA on root is "recommended". That's out of date: it's required.
- My plan: passkey on the root user, write down where the recovery stuff lives, and then basically never
  touch root again.
shaky: 'Root user' vs 'root' on Linux or a rooted phone: same word, and I'm not sure how far the 'full control' comparison really goes.
If root can do everything, can anything restrict it at all? For a standalone account like ours it sounds like basically no, which is exactly why MFA is required.

  30 services are always free.

  - **Free plan**: no charges at all. It ends after 6 months or when the credits run out, whichever comes
    first. Then the account *closes*. AWS keeps your content for 90 days, and you can upgrade to Paid in that
    window.
  - **Paid plan**: all services, pay-as-you-go once the credits are gone.

  tutorials are describing the legacy setup.
- **AWS Budgets**: set a cost or usage budget and get alerts (email) on actual and *forecasted* spend. Budget
  data updates up to 3 times a day, so alerts lag behind real spend.
- **Cost Explorer**: look back up to 13 months and forecast 12 months ahead.
- **AWS Pricing Calculator**: estimate costs before building anything.
- Stuff I set up in a Region I'm not looking at is easy to forget about. Check all of them.

On the Free plan you 'can't be charged', but the account closes after 6 months unless you upgrade. I did not expect that.
Tutorials saying '12 months free' are only right for legacy accounts, I think. I need to check which kind we're on.

Account day. Today was about the account itself and the scary all-powerful login.

- A new AWS account starts with exactly one identity: the **root user**. That's the email and password I
  signed up with, and it has complete access to every service and resource in the account.
- The account itself is identified by a 12-digit **account ID**.
- Rule number one: don't use root for everyday work. Save it for the root-only tasks, like changing the
  account's email or the root password, closing the account, and some billing and tax settings. What to use
  *instead* for daily work, I don't know yet. I'm guessing the IAM days get into it somehow?
- **MFA on root is required now**, for every kind of account. You have to register it within 35 days of your
  first console sign-in attempt.
- Supported MFA types:
  - passkeys and security keys (FIDO), which AWS recommends
  - virtual authenticator apps (the 6-digit TOTP codes)
  - hardware TOTP tokens

  touch root again.

- AWS rents out computing resources (servers, storage, databases and a lot more) and you pay for what you
  use, pay-as-you-go, instead of buying hardware up front. The docs also keep saying "elasticity": scale up
  when you need more, scale back down when you don't.
- Every capability is its own **service** with its own name. Signing up gives you access to all of them, and
  you're only charged for what you actually use. Names on our roadmap: IAM (days 3 to 6), S3 (from day 7),
  EC2 (from day 11). I don't know what they do yet, just that they're coming.
- Four ways to talk to AWS:
  1. the **AWS Management Console** (the website)
  2. the **AWS CLI** (command line)
  3. **SDKs** (code libraries; boto3 is the Python one)
  4. the raw **HTTP APIs**
- Big realisation: the console itself calls the same APIs. They're all different front-ends to the same
  thing, not different products.
- Every request to AWS gets signed (Signature Version 4, "SigV4") so AWS can tell who sent it, unless the
  request is anonymous. The CLI and SDKs do the signing for me. What the signing actually uses is something I
  haven't got to yet.
- Deployment models: all-in cloud, on-premises (your own data centre), or hybrid (a mix of both).
shaky: I half-assumed the CLI was more powerful than the console. If they all call the same APIs, is anything actually CLI-only? Not sure yet.
I know the cloud is just someone else's data centres, but I still catch myself picturing something vague and magical.

Global infrastructure notes.

- A **Region** is a separate geographic area, designed to be isolated from the other Regions. They have codes
  like us-east-1 (N. Virginia) and eu-west-1 (Ireland).
- Most resources are **regional**: you pick a Region and you only see that Region's stuff. AWS doesn't copy
  things between Regions for you.
- Each Region has **at least three Availability Zones (AZs)**. An AZ is "one or more discrete data centers",
  each with redundant power, networking and connectivity, in separate facilities. AZs in a Region are linked
  by low-latency fibre and don't share single points of failure.
- AZ names are the Region code plus a letter, like us-east-2a. There's also an **AZ ID**, like use2-az1,
  which is the same physical AZ in every account.
- Three flavours of resource: **zonal** (lives in one AZ), **regional**, and **global** (not tied to any
  Region). For high availability you spread across several AZs. Which things are which, I'll learn as I meet
  them.
- Choosing a Region: latency (be close to your users), cost, compliance and data residency, and whether the
  service you need is offered there. Some Regions are opt-in.
- Scale right now: 39 Regions, 124 AZs, 750+ edge points of presence. Saudi Arabia and Chile are announced.
- Edge locations (points of presence) are a different kind of site, not Regions. The service that uses
  them isn't on our plan, so I stopped there. Local Zones and Wavelength Zones also exist; I only skimmed those.
shaky: An AZ is not the same as a data centre. One AZ can be several data centres, and I keep forgetting that.

us-east-1a in my account might not be the same physical AZ as us-east-1a in yours, but only for older accounts in the oldest Regions; accounts from Nov 2025 get the same mapping. So that's why AZ IDs exist?
Apparently when stuff 'disappears' in the console, it's usually just the wrong Region selected. I bet I'll do this at least once.
